newsitem.title: FRANCE: French judge rejects 80-page cut in Bardot memoirs.
newsitem.headline: French judge rejects 80-page cut in Bardot memoirs.

text.p: A French judge on Thursday rejected a request by the son and an ex-husband of film star Brigitte Bardot to excise passages from her memoirs branding the baby a "tumour" and his father a "vulgar macho".

Judge Alain Lacabarats, who rules on emergency matters, threw out their request for immediate action. Another court will rule separately on December 4 on whether cuts should be made at all and whether the two should receive damages.

Bardot's son and ex-spouse had requested that 80 pages be slashed from her 555-page "Initiales B.B." under strict French laws governing privacy. The book, published a month ago, has already sold close to 400,000 copies.
Bardot, 62, now an animal rights campaigner, recounted in detail how she felt suicidal when she learnt she was pregnant with Nicolas and described him as "a tumour feeding off me".

The often bitter autobiography branded Nicolas' father Jacques, an actor-turned-producer who was married to Bardot from 1959 to 1963, "a vulgar, dictatorial and uncontrolled macho, a gigolo, alcoholic and despicable".
The actress was later reconciled with Nicolas, 36, her only son, who now lives in Norway.

"It is possible that the statements could harm the private life of (Charrier)," the judge said in his ruling, but he added that withdrawing the disputed pages would have no effect given the huge sales of the book.
At a hearing a week ago, the Charriers' lawyer urged the court to excise a string of passages from future editions of the book both in France and abroad.
The lawyer read out Bardot's letters to Jacques Charrier, second of her four husbands, during her pregnancy declaring her love for him and said the star was a "liar" for denouncing him in her book.

Bardot has said she regretted the court battle. Her lawyer argued that the life of Brigitte Bardot and Jacques Charrier was part of the history of France, and writings about historical events could not be banned.

Under French law, a special judge rules on urgent requests such as seizing books or halting a publication that is causing damage. An ordinary court then rules on the request, with time to look more carefully into all legal aspects of the case.
